title: Composition of Body Fluids and Compartments

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying body fluid compartments. The diagram below summarizes the '60-40-20 rule' for total body water distribution in a healthy adult man. Approximately what fraction of total body weight is represented by total body water (TBW)?
questions.diagram:
60-40-20 rule (healthy adult man)
TBW ≈ 60% of body weight (42 L in 70-kg man)
ICF ≈ 40% of body weight (~28 L; ~⅔ of TBW)
ECF ≈ 20% of body weight (~14 L; ~⅓ of TBW)
Within ECF: interstitial ~75% (~10.5 L), plasma ~25% (~3.5 L)
Women: ~50% TBW (more body fat); infants: ~75% (less fat); obese: lower TBW%
explanations: Correct. Total body water represents approximately 60% of body weight in adult men, with predictable variations: women have ~50% (higher fat percentage; adipose contains less water than lean tissue), infants have ~75% (relatively less fat), elderly have ~50–55% (lean mass loss), and obese individuals have lower percentage TBW (more adipose, less lean tissue). The '60-40-20 rule' summarizes the major compartments in healthy adult men: TBW = 60%, ICF = 40%, ECF = 20% of body weight. Within ECF, interstitial fluid is ~75% (~10.5 L) and plasma volume is ~25% (~3.5 L) in a 70-kg man.
Incorrect. 10% would be drastically below the actual TBW.
Incorrect. 30% is too low; it approximates ECF only.
Incorrect. 85% is too high for adults (though approaches infant TBW values).
Incorrect. The body is not 100% water.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is being evaluated for fluid management decisions. Compared with a 25-year-old man, which of the following best characterizes her likely total body water as a percentage of body weight?
choices: Higher TBW% than the young man
Lower TBW% than the young man
TBW% is determined entirely by genetics regardless of age or sex
explanations: Incorrect. Elderly women have LOWER TBW% than young men.

Correct. Women have lower TBW% than men due to higher body fat percentage (adipose tissue is poorly hydrated). Elderly individuals have lower TBW% than younger individuals due to sarcopenia (loss of lean muscle mass, which holds intracellular water) and loss of intracellular hydration. An elderly woman may have TBW ~45% of body weight versus ~60% in a young man. Clinically: elderly women are particularly vulnerable to dehydration with relatively small fluid losses (smaller absolute reserve), and to volume overload from over-resuscitation. Estimating fluid deficits and replacements requires accounting for these compartmental differences.
Incorrect. Sex and age both influence TBW%.
Incorrect. Sex, age, and body composition predictably affect TBW%.
Incorrect. TBW% DECREASES with age.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist measures the principal ions in intracellular fluid (ICF) and extracellular fluid (ECF). Which of the following correctly characterizes the principal cation of intracellular fluid?
choices: Na+ (the principal cation of ECF, not ICF)
Ca2+ (concentrated in extracellular fluid; intracellular Ca2+ is held very low by SERCA and PMCA pumps)
Mg2+ (the second most abundant intracellular cation but not the principal one)
H+ (mostly intracellular but at very low absolute concentration)
explanations: Incorrect. Na+ is the principal CATION of ECF, not ICF; intracellular Na+ is kept low by Na+/K+-ATPase.

Incorrect. Ca2+ is concentrated EXTRACELLULARLY (~2.5 mEq/L in plasma) and intracellularly is kept at very low (~10⁻⁷ M) levels by SERCA (sarcoplasmic reticulum) and PMCA (plasma membrane) Ca2+-ATPases.

Correct. K+ is the principal cation of intracellular fluid: intracellular [K+] ~140 mEq/L vs extracellular [K+] ~4 mEq/L. This 35:1 gradient is established by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, which pumps 3 Na+ OUT of cells in exchange for 2 K+ IN. The K+ gradient sets the resting membrane potential of excitable tissues (RMP ≈ −90 mV in skeletal muscle, close to the K+ equilibrium potential). Disruption of K+ distribution (hyperkalemia, hypokalemia) profoundly affects cardiac and neuromuscular function.
Incorrect. Mg2+ is the SECOND most abundant intracellular cation (~10–20 mEq/L), not the principal one.
Incorrect. H+ is present at very low concentrations (~40 nM intracellular) and is not a principal cation of either compartment.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist measures the composition of the extracellular fluid. Which of the following correctly characterizes the principal anion of extracellular fluid?
choices: HCO3− (the secondary ECF anion at ~24 mEq/L; second to chloride)
Protein anions (intracellular and contribute to anion gap)
explanations: Incorrect. Phosphate is the principal INTRACELLULAR anion (organic and inorganic phosphate as HPO4²⁻ and H2PO4⁻).
Incorrect. Sulfate is a minor anion in ECF.
Incorrect. HCO3− is the SECOND most abundant anion of ECF; chloride is more abundant.

Correct. Chloride (~100–106 mEq/L) is the principal anion of ECF, and along with bicarbonate (~24 mEq/L) accounts for most of the ECF anion charge balance against sodium (~140 mEq/L). The anion gap (Na+ − [Cl− + HCO3−]) reflects unmeasured anions (principally albumin and phosphate) and is normally 8–12 mEq/L.
Incorrect. Plasma proteins contribute to the anion gap but are not the principal anion of ECF in mass terms.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is comparing plasma versus interstitial fluid composition. Which of the following best describes the principal difference between plasma and interstitial fluid?
choices: Plasma has much more Na+ than interstitial fluid
Interstitial fluid has more K+ than plasma
Plasma has more Ca2+ than interstitial fluid
Plasma has more glucose than interstitial fluid
Plasma has more protein than interstitial fluid
explanations: Incorrect. Na+ concentration is essentially equal between plasma and interstitial fluid.
Incorrect. K+ concentration is essentially equal between plasma and interstitial fluid (both are extracellular).
Incorrect. Total Ca2+ in plasma is slightly higher than interstitial only because some plasma Ca2+ is bound to albumin; ionized Ca2+ is essentially equal.
Incorrect. Glucose concentration is essentially equal between plasma and interstitial fluid.

Correct. Plasma and interstitial fluid have essentially equal concentrations of Na+, K+, Cl−, HCO3−, glucose, and most small solutes — because the capillary endothelium freely permits small-molecule exchange (the Gibbs-Donnan effect produces small relative differences but they are negligible clinically). The principal difference is PROTEIN content: plasma contains albumin (~3.5–5 g/dL) and globulins, while interstitial fluid contains very little protein. This protein concentration gradient generates plasma oncotic pressure (~25 mm Hg), which opposes capillary filtration. The Starling force balance (Pgc, Pbs, πgc, πbs) determines net fluid movement across capillary walls; loss of plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., severe hypoalbuminemia in nephrotic syndrome) shifts fluid into the interstitium, producing edema.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a serum sodium 140 mEq/L, glucose 90 mg/dL, and BUN 14 mg/dL. The clinician calculates plasma osmolality from these values. Which of the following formulas correctly approximates calculated plasma osmolality?
explanations: Correct. Standard estimated plasma osmolality formula: Posm ≈ 2 × Na+ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (where glucose and BUN are in mg/dL and Na+ in mEq/L). The 2× factor on Na+ accounts for accompanying anions (Cl−, HCO3−). Glucose/18 converts mg/dL to mOsm/kg (the molecular weight of glucose is 180; so 18 = MW/10). BUN/2.8 converts mg/dL to mOsm/kg (the molecular weight of urea is 60, but BUN measures only the nitrogen content; 2.8 = MW(urea) / [MW(nitrogen × 2)] simplified). Calculated osmolality typically agrees with measured to within 10 mOsm/kg; a larger 'osmolar gap' suggests unmeasured solutes such as mannitol (during therapy), ethanol, methanol, or ethylene glycol (toxic alcohols).
Incorrect. Sodium alone underestimates osmolality; the formula multiplies by 2 for accompanying anions.
Incorrect. K+ and Cl− are not in the standard formula.
Incorrect. This is dimensionally incorrect.
Incorrect. Albumin contributes minimally to osmolality (large molecule, low mole fraction).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old physiologist is comparing plasma osmolality, plasma osmolarity, and tonicity. Which of the following correctly distinguishes osmolarity from tonicity?
choices: Tonicity considers only effective osmoles that don't cross cell membranes
Tonicity is independent of any solute composition
Tonicity is always lower than osmolarity
explanations: Incorrect. Osmolarity and tonicity are RELATED but distinct concepts.

Correct. The distinction is critical: osmolarity is the TOTAL concentration of osmotically active particles in solution (mOsm/L); osmolality (mOsm/kg) is essentially the same. TONICITY refers only to the effective osmoles — those that do NOT freely cross cell membranes — and therefore generate a SUSTAINED osmotic gradient that changes cell volume. Sodium (which doesn't equilibrate quickly across cell membranes) and glucose (in low-insulin states, doesn't equilibrate) are EFFECTIVE osmoles. Urea is an INEFFECTIVE osmole because it freely crosses cell membranes (equilibrates between ECF and ICF), so it raises osmolality WITHOUT changing tonicity or cell volume. Clinical implication: a uremic patient with high BUN has elevated plasma osmolality but no tonicity disturbance — and no neurologic symptoms from osmotic shift, distinguishing this from hypernatremia (an effective osmole disturbance).
Incorrect. Tonicity DOES depend on solute composition (specifically, which solutes cross membranes).
Incorrect. Tonicity can be equal to or lower than osmolarity (depending on contribution of ineffective osmoles).
Incorrect. Osmolarity considers ALL osmotically active particles (ionized AND uncharged).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher wants to measure total body water in a study volunteer using indicator dilution. Which of the following substances is most appropriate as a TBW marker?
explanations: Incorrect. Inulin distributes through ECF only (it does not enter cells); used to measure ECF, not TBW.
Incorrect. Evans blue dye binds to albumin and remains within plasma; used to measure plasma volume, not TBW.

Correct. Tritiated water (³H₂O), deuterium oxide (D₂O), and antipyrine are classic markers for total body water. They distribute uniformly throughout ICF + ECF (and fat to a lesser extent) because they cross cell membranes freely and behave similarly to water itself. After IV administration and equilibration (~1 hour for ³H₂O), TBW is calculated by indicator dilution: TBW = (administered dose × 100) / (plasma concentration after equilibration).
Incorrect. Mannitol distributes through ECF only; it is too large to enter cells.
Incorrect. Albumin remains within plasma.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist wants to measure the extracellular fluid (ECF) volume in a research subject. Which of the following substances is an appropriate marker for ECF measurement?
choices: Tritiated water (³H₂O) — distributes through TBW, not just ECF
Evans blue dye — binds to albumin and stays in plasma
Glucose — enters cells in insulin-dependent tissues
explanations: Incorrect. ³H₂O distributes through TBW (ICF + ECF), not just ECF.
Incorrect. Evans blue stays in plasma (used for plasma volume).
Incorrect. Radiolabeled albumin stays in plasma.

Correct. Markers for ECF measurement include inulin (a polysaccharide), mannitol, sucrose, and sulfate (²²Na-thiosulfate or ³⁵SO4²⁻). These substances distribute through the extracellular space — plasma + interstitial fluid — but do not enter cells. After IV administration and equilibration, ECF volume = (dose × 100) / (plasma concentration after equilibration). Intracellular fluid volume is then calculated by subtraction: ICF = TBW − ECF, using the TBW measurement from a separate marker like tritiated water.
Incorrect. Glucose enters insulin-dependent cells (skeletal muscle, adipose); it is not an ECF marker.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher wants to measure plasma volume in a clinical research subject. Which of the following substances is an appropriate marker for plasma volume?
choices: Evans blue dye or radioiodinated serum albumin
explanations: Incorrect. Tritiated water measures TBW.
Incorrect. Inulin measures ECF (plasma + interstitial).
Incorrect. Mannitol measures ECF.
Incorrect. Glucose enters cells and is not a compartment marker.

Correct. Markers for plasma volume measurement include Evans blue dye and radioiodinated serum albumin (RISA, labeled with ¹²⁵I or ¹³¹I). Both bind to albumin, which is largely confined to plasma (very small amount in interstitial fluid). After IV administration and equilibration (rapid for albumin), plasma volume = (dose × 100) / (plasma concentration). Interstitial fluid volume is calculated by subtraction: ISF = ECF (from inulin/mannitol) − plasma volume.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher injects 3 mg of inulin IV into a study volunteer. After equilibration, the plasma inulin concentration is 0.02 mg/dL. Assuming complete equilibration in the ECF and no urinary loss in the brief equilibration period, what is the patient's ECF volume?
choices: Cannot be determined without knowing TBW
explanations: Correct. ECF = (dose × 100) / (plasma concentration in mg/dL) = (3 mg × 100) / 0.02 mg/dL = 15,000 mL = 15 L. This is in the expected range for an average adult (ECF ~14 L; 20% of 70 kg). The calculation assumes complete equilibration of inulin in the ECF, no significant urinary loss during the equilibration window, and that inulin distributes only in ECF (not into cells). The factor of 100 converts dL to mL.
Incorrect. 1.5 L is far below the expected ECF volume.
Incorrect. 150 mL is grossly too small.
Incorrect. 150 L is impossibly large.
Incorrect. ECF can be calculated from inulin dose and plasma concentration without knowing TBW.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist studies the four Starling forces governing fluid movement across systemic capillaries. Which of the following best describes net fluid movement at a typical systemic capillary?
choices: Fluid filters at the arteriolar end and reabsorbs at the venular end
explanations: Correct. The four Starling forces at systemic capillaries: (1) capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) ~30 mm Hg arteriolar end / ~15 mm Hg venular end; (2) plasma colloid osmotic pressure (πp) ~25 mm Hg; (3) interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi) ~−2 mm Hg (slightly negative); (4) interstitial colloid osmotic pressure (πi) ~5 mm Hg. Net pressure = (Pc − Pi) − (πp − πi). At the arteriolar end, Pc dominates (filtration into interstitium); at the venular end, πp dominates (reabsorption back into capillary). About 90% of filtered fluid is reabsorbed at the venular end; the ~10% remainder is cleared by lymphatics. This balance permits ongoing nutrient/waste exchange between blood and tissue without net fluid accumulation. Imbalances (raised Pc in HF; lowered πp in nephrotic syndrome; lymphatic obstruction; increased capillary permeability) produce edema.
Incorrect. Capillaries permit both filtration and reabsorption.
Incorrect. Capillaries permit both filtration and reabsorption.
Incorrect. Capillaries are highly permeable to water and small solutes.
Incorrect. Capillaries do not actively pump fluid; movement is passive (driven by Starling forces).

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with chronic systolic heart failure has bilateral lower-extremity edema. Which of the following best describes the principal Starling-force abnormality producing his edema?
explanations: Incorrect. Plasma oncotic pressure is typically NORMAL in HF unless concurrent malnutrition or severe protein loss exists.

Incorrect. Lymphatic obstruction (e.g., from filariasis, surgery, or malignancy) causes lymphedema with characteristic features (non-pitting, predominantly distal); HF edema is mainly venous-pressure-driven.

Correct. In right-sided HF (or biventricular HF), the principal mechanism of peripheral edema is INCREASED CAPILLARY HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE. Elevated central venous pressure (from impaired cardiac output) transmits retrograde through the venous system to systemic capillaries; capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, shifting the Starling balance toward filtration. Lymphatics initially compensate by clearing excess interstitial fluid, but eventually become overwhelmed → peripheral edema. The same mechanism in left-sided HF causes pulmonary congestion: elevated pulmonary venous pressure → elevated pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure → fluid filtration into alveoli (pulmonary edema). Reduced effective arterial volume in HF activates RAAS, SNS, and ADH, driving Na+ and water retention that further raises capillary hydrostatic pressures.
Incorrect. Increased capillary permeability is not the primary mechanism in HF; it characterizes inflammatory/septic edema.
Incorrect. Interstitial oncotic pressure is not typically the dominant abnormality in HF.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis presents with anasarca. Laboratory studies are shown.

labs.name: Examination
labs.value: 3+ pitting LE edema, periorbital edema, ascites

choices: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from heart failure
explanations: Incorrect. There is no evidence of HF; the principal abnormality is heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia.
Incorrect. Lymphatic obstruction produces non-pitting lymphedema, typically asymmetric.
Incorrect. Sepsis-related capillary leak produces a different clinical picture (fever, hemodynamic instability).

Correct. Nephrotic syndrome edema results principally from REDUCED PLASMA COLLOID OSMOTIC PRESSURE: urinary albumin loss lowers serum albumin and plasma oncotic pressure (typically <2 g/dL produces meaningful fluid shift). The reduced oncotic pressure shifts the Starling balance toward filtration into the interstitium → edema. In addition, modern thinking emphasizes a coexisting 'overfill' mechanism: filtered plasmin in heavy proteinuria activates apical ENaC in the collecting duct, producing primary tubular Na+ retention. Both 'underfill' and 'overfill' mechanisms typically operate together; the relative contribution varies (underfill more prominent in MCD/severe hypoalbuminemia; overfill more prominent in adult FSGS/membranous). Treatment: salt restriction, diuretics, treating the underlying disease (steroids, immunosuppressants).
Incorrect. RAS would produce hypertension and hyperaldosteronism but not the heavy proteinuria described.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with breast cancer underwent right axillary lymph node dissection 6 months ago. She now has progressive non-pitting swelling of her right arm without a corresponding left-sided change. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of her arm edema?
explanations: Incorrect. Capillary hydrostatic pressure is not the principal abnormality in lymphedema.
Incorrect. Plasma oncotic pressure is normal.
Incorrect. Capillary permeability is not the principal abnormality in lymphedema.
Incorrect. While interstitial oncotic pressure is elevated (from accumulated proteins that cannot be cleared), the primary problem is the lymphatic obstruction itself.

Correct. Lymphedema results from impaired lymphatic drainage. Normal capillary filtration produces a small interstitial protein load (proteins that leak across the capillary endothelium); lymphatics return this protein-rich fluid to the venous system. When lymphatic drainage is obstructed (post-surgical, post-radiation, post-infectious like filariasis, congenital), interstitial fluid AND protein accumulate. The edema is initially soft and pitting but becomes firm and non-pitting over months to years due to fibrosis. Distinctive features: usually unilateral or asymmetric; involves dorsum of hand/foot; characteristic 'Stemmer sign' (cannot pinch dorsal skin of toes/fingers). Worldwide leading cause is Wuchereria bancrofti (filariasis); in developed countries, post-surgical and post-radiation cases dominate. Treatment: compression, lymphedema drainage techniques, careful skin care.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with septic shock has bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, hypotension, and severe edema. Capillary leak is contributing to his fluid extravasation. Which of the following best describes the Starling-force abnormality in sepsis-related edema?
choices: Increased capillary permeability from inflammatory mediators
explanations: Correct. Septic capillary leak is principally driven by INCREASED CAPILLARY PERMEABILITY. Inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes) acting on capillary endothelium widen interendothelial junctions, allowing proteins to leak across — particularly albumin. This has two combined Starling effects: (1) plasma oncotic pressure falls because albumin is lost from plasma; (2) interstitial oncotic pressure RISES because albumin accumulates in interstitium. The combination shifts the Starling balance toward filtration. The result is massive interstitial edema that is poorly responsive to oncotic resuscitation alone (because added albumin also leaks into the interstitium). Severe septic capillary leak produces ARDS (lungs), anasarca (whole body), and circulatory shock. Management is challenging: fluid resuscitation balances the need to support cardiac output against the risk of worsening edema; balanced crystalloids preferred; vasopressors (norepinephrine) added for refractory hypotension.
Incorrect. Capillary permeability INCREASES in sepsis, not decreases.
Incorrect. Plasma oncotic pressure FALLS due to protein leak.
Incorrect. Capillary hydrostatic pressure is not principally the issue.
Incorrect. Lymphatic obstruction is not the mechanism in sepsis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher infuses 1 L of 0.9% normal saline IV into a healthy volunteer. Compared with pre-infusion baseline, which row in the table best characterizes the immediate (within 30 minutes) effects on body fluid compartments?
explanations: Correct. 0.9% saline (NS) is iso-osmotic with plasma (~308 mOsm/L). When infused, it distributes throughout the EXTRACELLULAR FLUID (because Na+ does not freely cross cell membranes; Na+ is largely excluded from ICF). Approximately 75% of the infused volume goes to interstitial fluid and 25% stays in plasma (in proportion to ECF compartment ratios). ICF volume is UNCHANGED because there is no osmotic gradient to drive water shift between ICF and ECF. Net effect: TBW ↑ by 1 L, ECF ↑ by 1 L, ICF unchanged. This is why isotonic saline is preferred for volume resuscitation in hypovolemia (replaces ECF without changing ICF). Distinct from D5W (free water, distributes proportionally to TBW with both ECF and ICF gains).
Incorrect. Isotonic NaCl does not enter cells; ICF is unchanged.
Incorrect. ECF gains volume; not the opposite.
Incorrect. Infusing 1 L produces measurable changes; values are not unchanged.
Incorrect. Infusing fluid increases (not decreases) volumes.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher infuses 1 L of 5% dextrose in water (D5W) IV into a healthy volunteer. The dextrose is rapidly metabolized to CO2 and water, leaving essentially free water as the net infused load. Compared with pre-infusion baseline, which row in the table best characterizes the immediate effects on body fluid compartments after dextrose metabolism?
explanations: Correct. D5W is essentially free water once dextrose is metabolized to CO2 and water (the dextrose is metabolized within minutes by tissues). Free water distributes throughout TOTAL BODY WATER in proportion to compartment sizes: ICF (~⅔ of TBW) gets ~⅔ of the infused volume; ECF (~⅓ of TBW) gets ~⅓. After 1 L D5W, ICF rises by ~667 mL and ECF rises by ~333 mL. Plasma volume rises by only ~83 mL (25% of ECF gain). Because so little stays in plasma, D5W is INEFFECTIVE for resuscitating hypovolemic shock; it is used primarily for free water replacement (e.g., correction of hypernatremic dehydration) or as a vehicle for medications.
Incorrect. D5W (free water) DOES enter cells; ICF rises.
Incorrect. ECF rises (~⅓ of infused water), not falls.
Incorrect. ICF rises (~⅔ of infused water), not falls.
Incorrect. Infusing 1 L produces measurable changes; values are not unchanged.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with severely symptomatic hyponatremia (Na 112 mEq/L, seizure) receives 100 mL of 3% hypertonic saline IV. Compared with isotonic saline, which of the following best describes the effect of hypertonic saline on body fluid compartments?
choices: Hypertonic saline distributes purely in ICF
3% saline expands ECF and contracts ICF
Hypertonic saline is iso-osmotic with plasma
Hypertonic saline expands ICF more than ECF
explanations: Incorrect. Hypertonic saline distributes in ECF (Na+ does not enter cells freely); it does not enter ICF.

Correct. 3% saline (513 mEq/L) is approximately 3.5× the osmolality of plasma. When infused, it raises ECF osmolality and creates an osmotic gradient across cell membranes (Na+ does not cross freely). Water shifts from ICF INTO ECF, expanding ECF beyond the infused volume and contracting ICF. The plasma sodium concentration rises rapidly. This is the basis for using hypertonic saline in severely symptomatic hyponatremia (with seizures or coma): 100 mL of 3% saline raises plasma Na+ by ~2–3 mEq/L within 30 minutes, and can be repeated up to total correction of 4–6 mEq/L in the first few hours (limited to ≤8 mEq/L total in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome). Hypertonic saline is also used in cerebral edema for similar volume effects on brain water.
Incorrect. Hypertonic saline EXPANDS ECF volume.
Incorrect. 3% saline is HYPERTONIC, not iso-osmotic with plasma.
Incorrect. Hypertonic saline expands ECF (and contracts ICF), not the reverse.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted 5 days after pituitary surgery for craniopharyngioma. She has been confused and lethargic for 24 hours, with markedly reduced PO intake. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Central diabetes insipidus with pure water loss
explanations: Incorrect. SIADH produces euvolemic HYPOnatremia with concentrated urine; this patient has hypernatremia with dilute urine.
Incorrect. Extra-renal losses with water replacement could produce HYPOnatremia, not hypernatremia.

Correct. Central DI from pituitary surgery is the diagnosis. The water-deprivation/desmopressin response is classic: DI patients fail to concentrate urine despite dehydration and rising plasma osmolality (urine osm 85 with plasma osm 352 confirms inappropriate dilute urine); desmopressin restores urine concentration (rises to 580), confirming central rather than nephrogenic DI. Compartment effects of pure water loss: TBW falls in proportion to all compartments (since water freely crosses cell membranes), so most absolute water loss is from ICF (the largest compartment). Plasma sodium concentration RISES because the residual Na+ is now in less water. Plasma osmolality rises. Treatment: free water replacement (oral preferred; IV D5W or hypotonic saline if NPO; calculate water deficit) AND desmopressin to stop ongoing renal water loss. Correction must be slow (≤10 mEq/L/24h) to avoid cerebral edema.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease but presents with HYPOnatremia and HYPOvolemia (sodium-driven water loss).
Incorrect. Sweat losses are hypotonic but rarely produce 8 L/day of polyuria with dilute urine.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man presents with vomiting and watery diarrhea for 3 days, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension. Laboratory studies show plasma sodium 132 mEq/L, BUN:creatinine ratio 28, urine sodium 8 mEq/L. Which of the following best describes the body fluid compartment effect of hypotonic NaCl loss with disproportionate water replacement (drinking water but not electrolytes)?
choices: Isotonic volume loss without compartment shift
Hypotonic Na+ losses with disproportionate water replacement
explanations: Incorrect. This patient has HYPOnatremia, not hypernatremia; the compartment shift is opposite of pure water loss.
Incorrect. The patient has GI Na+ AND water losses, with disproportionate water replacement — not pure free water loss.
Incorrect. There is a compartment shift; ICF rises (paradoxically) and ECF contracts.

Correct. The classical pattern of hypotonic Na+ loss (vomiting, diarrhea) with disproportionate water replacement (drinking water alone). Gastric and intestinal fluid Na+ ~120–130 mEq/L (slightly hypotonic to plasma 140). Each liter lost removes ~120 mEq Na+ + 1 L water. Replacement with plain water adds water without Na+. Cumulative: ECF Na+ deficit is partially repaired by water shifting from ECF compartments and from drinking water mass entering TBW; but the water replacement disproportionately enters ICF (since water distributes per TBW, ⅔ to ICF). End result: ECF VOLUME is contracted (orthostatic hypotension, prerenal azotemia, low UNa); ICF VOLUME is expanded; plasma SODIUM is low (because more water than Na+ has been replaced). Treatment: isotonic saline replaces both volume and Na+ deficit; plasma Na+ corrects as water excess is distributed proportionally.
Incorrect. Total volume is contracted, not expanded; the patient has hemodynamic signs of hypovolemia.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man arrives in the emergency department with class III hemorrhagic shock from a stab wound. He has lost approximately 1.5 L of blood (~30% of plasma volume). Which of the following best describes the immediate body fluid compartment effects of acute hemorrhage?
choices: Plasma volume only is reduced; ECF and ICF unchanged
Hemorrhage causes ICF expansion through cellular oncotic shift
Acute hemorrhage is an isotonic ECF volume loss
explanations: Incorrect. Plasma volume is the principally affected compartment, but ECF as a whole falls because plasma is part of ECF.
Incorrect. Hemorrhage does not produce ICF expansion; ICF volume is unchanged.
Incorrect. Hemorrhage is an ISOTONIC loss, not hypotonic.
Incorrect. Crystalloid resuscitation is the standard initial approach; colloid can be added for severe or refractory shock.

Correct. Acute blood loss is an ISOTONIC volume loss because blood is iso-osmotic with plasma. The immediate compartment effects: (1) plasma volume is reduced (the actual lost compartment); (2) total ECF falls because plasma is part of ECF; (3) ICF is UNCHANGED because plasma osmolality is unaffected (no osmotic gradient drives water shift between ICF and ECF); (4) plasma sodium remains in normal range. Over the next hours, transcapillary refill from the interstitium partially restores plasma volume (the so-called 'autotransfusion' effect); plasma proteins also redistribute. Initial resuscitation: isotonic crystalloid (NS, LR) for moderate loss; blood products (packed red cells, plasma, platelets) for severe loss in 1:1:1 ratio. Hemoglobin falls only after volume restoration reveals the dilution.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops euvolemic hyponatremia (Na 122) from SIADH. Plasma osmolality is 252 mOsm/kg. Which of the following best describes the principal compartment effect of pure water gain?
choices: Pure water gain expands all compartments, predominantly ICF
Pure water gain expands only ECF
Pure water gain expands only ICF
Pure water gain does not change compartment volumes
explanations: Correct. SIADH produces a state of pure water gain (free water retained because of inappropriate ADH-driven AQP2-mediated reabsorption in the collecting duct). The retained free water distributes throughout TBW per compartment proportions: ICF (~⅔ of TBW) gains the majority; ECF (~⅓) gains the minor share. Plasma sodium concentration falls (Na+ is now diluted in more water); plasma osmolality falls. ECF volume rises modestly — typically not enough to produce overt edema or hypertension (hence 'euvolemic'). ICF volume rises substantially, INCLUDING brain cells. Cerebral edema from ICF expansion is responsible for the neurologic symptoms of severe hyponatremia: confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma. Chronic hyponatremia is partly compensated by brain idiogenic osmole loss (myo-inositol, glutamine), which is why correction must be SLOW (≤8 mEq/L/24h) to avoid osmotic demyelination from rapid water shift back out of brain cells. Treatment: free water restriction; V2 antagonist (tolvaptan); hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic.
Incorrect. Free water expands ALL compartments, not just ECF.
Incorrect. Free water expands ALL compartments; ECF gains ~⅓ of the volume.
Incorrect. Free water gain produces measurable changes in compartment volumes.
Incorrect. Pure water gain produces HYPONATREMIA (low Na+ concentration), not hypernatremia.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with HFrEF has gained 8 kg of fluid weight, has elevated jugular venous pressure, and has 3+ pitting lower-extremity edema. He has avid renal Na+ retention with FENa <0.5%. Which of the following best describes the body fluid compartment effect of isotonic NaCl gain?
choices: Isotonic Na+ retention produces ICF expansion only
Isotonic Na+ retention expands ECF without changing ICF
Isotonic Na+ retention is the same as pure water retention
explanations: Incorrect. Na+ does not enter cells; ICF is unchanged.

Correct. Isotonic Na+ gain is the cardinal pattern of HF, cirrhosis with ascites, primary hyperaldosteronism, and apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Retained Na+ stays within ECF (since Na+ does not freely cross cell membranes); water follows osmotically and also stays in ECF (no osmotic gradient drives water into ICF). Plasma sodium concentration is essentially unchanged (the retained Na+ comes with proportional water). ECF EXPANSION manifests clinically as: weight gain, peripheral edema, elevated JVP, pulmonary congestion (left HF), ascites (cirrhosis), pleural effusions. ICF is unchanged. Treatment: salt restriction, diuretics (loop, thiazide, mineralocorticoid antagonists), treating underlying disease.
Incorrect. Isotonic Na+ retention EXPANDS, not contracts, ECF.
Incorrect. Plasma Na+ concentration is essentially unchanged because the retained Na+ comes with proportional water.
Incorrect. Pure water retention expands all compartments and causes hyponatremia; isotonic Na+ retention expands only ECF and does not change Na+ concentration.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with new-onset DKA has plasma glucose 580 mg/dL and plasma sodium 131 mEq/L. The plasma sodium is below normal. Which of the following best explains the apparent hyponatremia in this patient?
explanations: Incorrect. SIADH features euvolemic hyponatremia with low PLASMA OSMOLALITY; this patient has HIGH plasma osmolality from glucose.
Incorrect. CSW occurs in CNS disease, not DKA.

Correct. In hyperglycemia (and during mannitol therapy), translational hyponatremia occurs because the hypertonic plasma draws water out of cells into ECF, diluting plasma sodium WITHOUT changing total body sodium. Glucose is an EFFECTIVE osmole in low-insulin states because cellular glucose uptake is impaired, so the glucose stays in ECF and exerts osmotic pull. Plasma OSMOLALITY is HIGH (not low) in hyperglycemic hyponatremia, distinguishing it from dilutional hyponatremia. The CORRECTION formula: Na+ corrected = Na+ measured + 1.6 × (glucose − 100)/100 (for every 100 mg/dL glucose above 100, Na+ is depressed by ~1.6 mEq/L). For glucose 580 and Na+ 131: corrected Na+ = 131 + 1.6 × 4.8 = ~139 (normal). With insulin therapy, glucose falls, water shifts back into cells, and plasma Na+ rises toward normal. This 'translational' hyponatremia is benign and does not require Na+ replacement — just glucose correction.
Incorrect. Pseudohyponatremia has NORMAL plasma osmolality (a laboratory artifact); this patient has HIGH plasma osmolality.
Incorrect. AKI does not principally cause hyponatremia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher places isolated kidney cells in solutions of varying tonicity. Which of the following correctly characterizes the response of cells to a HYPERTONIC solution?
choices: Cells swell because water moves OUT of solution INTO cells
Cells are unaffected by hypertonic solution
Cells shrink (crenate) as water moves out of cells
Cells become dense and dehydrated only after 24 hours
explanations: Incorrect. Water moves OUT of cells (toward higher solute concentration) in hypertonic solution; cells shrink, not swell.
Incorrect. Cell lysis occurs in HYPOTONIC solution (cells swell to bursting), not hypertonic.
Incorrect. Cells DO respond to tonicity changes via osmotic water shift.

Correct. The cellular volume response to tonicity is the basis for many physiologic and pathologic processes. In HYPERTONIC solution (higher effective osmole concentration than ICF), water moves OUT of cells to equilibrate the gradient — cells SHRINK (crenate in red cells, lose volume in other cell types). In HYPOTONIC solution, water moves INTO cells — cells SWELL (in red cells, can lyse if the stress is severe enough). In ISOTONIC solution, no osmotic gradient exists and cell volume is unchanged. Critical distinction: TONICITY refers to effective osmoles only — those that don't freely cross cell membranes. Urea, for example, raises osmolality but is NOT a tonicity factor (it equilibrates between ICF and ECF). This is why hyperosmolar uremic patients have NO osmotic shift, while equally osmolar hyperglycemic patients DO have osmotic shift (because glucose is an effective osmole when insulin-deficient).
Incorrect. Cellular volume response to tonicity is rapid (seconds-to-minutes), not 24 hours.
